name: Speakeasy
license: Proprietary service; CLI under the Elastic License 2.0; Gram under AGPL-3.0
summary: Generates typed SDKs, Terraform providers, CLIs and MCP servers from an OpenAPI document, and now also sells a hosted MCP platform and an enterprise MCP gateway that governs which agents may call which tools.
intro: Speakeasy started as an SDK generator, and that is still how most developers meet it. You point its CLI at an OpenAPI 3.0 or 3.1 document; `speakeasy quickstart` asks whether you want an SDK or an MCP server and in which language, then `speakeasy run` validates the spec, generates the code and compiles it. Generators exist for TypeScript, Python, Go, Java, C#, PHP and Ruby (Rust and C++ are marked “coming soon”), each written to be idiomatic: the TypeScript SDK uses `fetch`, validates every model with Zod and offers optional retries and pagination, and the Python one is built on Pydantic models. Changes to names or examples go in OpenAPI Overlays so the original spec stays untouched, and the output is meant to be committed to GitHub and regenerated in CI. Free accounts can generate one SDK of up to 50 API methods.

The same spec can become an MCP server. `speakeasy quickstart --mcp` writes a TypeScript server, optionally with a Cloudflare Worker config, or Speakeasy hosts it: every operation becomes a tool, regenerated on each push, behind OAuth with your identity provider or Speakeasy as the authorization server, and every call logged with the customer and client. That hosted platform grew out of Gram, which Speakeasy open-sourced in 2025.

Since 2026 the company sells itself mainly as an “AI control plane” for enterprises: an MCP gateway with an approved registry of servers, access provisioned from Okta or Entra ID by role, inspection of prompts and tool calls for PII and prompt injection, and an audit trail of every call. Its public pricing page lists only an Enterprise plan for this, priced by tool-call requests.
strengths: One OpenAPI document drives SDKs in seven languages, Terraform providers, a CLI and an MCP server, so they stay in step with the API
Idiomatic output: typed models (Zod in TypeScript, Pydantic in Python), with optional retries and pagination, rather than a generic template
Overlays keep customizations outside the spec, so regeneration in CI doesn’t lose them
A path from a generated MCP server to a hosted one with OAuth, per-customer logs and OpenTelemetry export
limits: Not open source: the CLI is under the Elastic License 2.0 and generation needs a Speakeasy account; the free tier covers one SDK of up to 50 methods
The output is only as good as the OpenAPI document, which often needs cleanup and overlays first
The company’s focus has moved to enterprise MCP governance, and that product has no public price
Its own pricing FAQ warns that model accuracy drops once a server exposes 30 to 40 tools, so a large API needs curation before it makes a good MCP server

snippet.title: Generate an SDK or an MCP server from an OpenAPI document
source: speakeasy quickstart        # sign in, give it an OpenAPI 3.x file or URL, pick SDK and a language
speakeasy quickstart --mcp  # or generate a TypeScript MCP server (optionally for Cloudflare Workers)
speakeasy run               # after the spec changes: validate, regenerate and compile

story: Sagar Batchu, Speakeasy’s co-founder and CEO, announced the company in June 2023 with $11 million in pre-seed and seed funding from backers including GV and Quiet Capital. The pitch was the “final mile” of API integration: companies like Stripe, Plaid and Twilio win users with polished SDKs, but most API teams cannot afford to build and maintain them in many languages, so Speakeasy would generate managed SDKs and Terraform providers from the API’s own description. By launch it said it had generated 4,000 SDKs across 8 languages.

In October 2024 it raised a $15 million Series A led by FPV Ventures, describing its aim as ending “API embarrassment”: stale docs, accidental breaking changes and SDKs that lag the API. As agents arrived, the same generators began emitting MCP servers, and in September 2025 Speakeasy put Gram into public beta, an open-source platform for curating API endpoints into a small set of well-described tools and hosting the resulting MCP servers.

In 2026 Speakeasy repositioned around governing AI use inside companies, publishing an “AI control plane” reference in April and selling an MCP gateway for registries, role-based access, inspection and audit. SDK generation continues alongside, with CLI releases still shipping every few days.

choices.choice: Generate from OpenAPI rather than ask teams to adopt a new schema
choices.why: Most API teams already have an OpenAPI description, so making it the single source let Speakeasy produce SDKs, Terraform providers and later MCP servers without changing how the API is built.
Speakeasy built each generator with language experts, using Zod in TypeScript and Pydantic in Python, because SDKs that feel foreign to a language community go unused.

choices.choice: Curate tools instead of exposing every endpoint
choices.why: Gram’s launch post argued that MCP servers fail when they expose too many tools without context, so it turns a 600-endpoint API into a focused set of 5 to 30 tools.
